A.explanation: Too small by about a factor of 5. It likely comes from a unit or area error, such as not converting $\text{mm}$ to $\text{m}$ correctly when finding the area under the tension-extension graph.

B.explanation: The increase in area under the graph from $100\text{ N}$ to $150\text{ N}$ is about $18.8\times 10^{-3}\text{ J}$, which is $19\text{ mJ}$.

C.explanation: About $34\text{ mJ}$ is the total elastic energy at $150\text{ N}$, given by $\frac{1}{2}\times 150\times 0.45\times 10^{-3}$, not the change from $100\text{ N}$.

D.explanation: About double the correct change. It comes from omitting the $\frac{1}{2}$ in $E=\frac{1}{2}Fx$ and using force times extension for the extra strip.

hints: Look at the tension against extension graph and read the extension at each tension: about $0.30\text{ mm}$ at $100\text{ N}$ and $0.45\text{ mm}$ at $150\text{ N}$.
Recall that elastic potential energy is the area under the tension-extension graph, so the gust adds only the narrow trapezoidal strip between $0.30\text{ mm}$ and $0.45\text{ mm}$.
Calculate $\frac{1}{2}Fx$ at $150\text{ N}$ and at $100\text{ N}$ after converting $\text{mm}$ to $\text{m}$, then subtract to find the increase.
walkthrough: Read the two states from the straight-line graph. At $100\text{ N}$ the extension is $0.30\text{ mm}$ and at $150\text{ N}$ the extension is $0.45\text{ mm}$.
Use the rule that elastic potential energy equals the area under the tension-extension graph. For this linear graph from the origin, $E = \frac{1}{2}Fx$.
Convert extensions to metres: $0.30\text{ mm}=0.30\times 10^{-3}\text{ m}$ and $0.45\text{ mm}=0.45\times 10^{-3}\text{ m}$.
Initial energy at $100\text{ N}$ is $E_1 = \frac{1}{2}\times 100\times 0.30\times 10^{-3} = 15.0\times 10^{-3}\text{ J}$.
Final energy at $150\text{ N}$ is $E_2 = \frac{1}{2}\times 150\times 0.45\times 10^{-3} = 33.75\times 10^{-3}\text{ J}$.
Change caused by the gust is $\Delta E = E_2 - E_1 = 18.75\times 10^{-3}\text{ J} \approx 19\text{ mJ}$. This is option B.
